titleStmt.title: Scheduling Analysis of Distributed Real-Time Systems Under Functional Constraints *

analytic.title: Scheduling Analysis of Distributed Real-Time Systems Under Functional Constraints *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Scheduling analysis for simplified distributed real-time systems, where the worst case execution time (WCET) of each task is fixed, is well understood. However, often the simplified assumption of fixed WCETs lacks accuracy, e.g. it may have a high variance depending on internal task states. Even if the transition relation of task's internal states is known, traditionally applied scalable analysis approaches cannot exploit this information in order to yield more accurate response times. In this paper we propose a new type of analysis for this kind of real-time systems. Our approach is based on a transformation of response time analysis into a satisfiability problem, enriched by task internal automata. Evaluations show the powerfulness of this analysis and, furthermore, we will exemplify how our approach can be used to analyse systems with mixed temporal and functional characterisations.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The timing analysis of distributed embedded real-time systems is key to reach safety related maturity gates, e.g. demanded for advanced driving assistant systems in automotive industry. Several analysis methods are available to fulfil this task for a variety of different underlying scheduling paradigms, like preemptive and time triggered scheduling. In general there exist two completely different approaches to safely assess temporal behaviour: analytical methods [1] and computational methods [2]. While the latter allow for powerful timing assessment which takes functional behaviour into account, they lack of scalability [3] and, even more restrictive, key temporal behaviour in general is undecidable [4]. Analytical methods on the other hand are very popular due to the integration of more and more complex run-time behaviour and environmen-tal behaviour [5,1,6] in the last twenty years. While they scale very well, these methods lack accuracy because of over-approximations introduced in order to allow for a corner case analysis capability. In the end such overapproximation leads to over-dimensioning the hardware resources, which in product-cost driven industry, like the automotive industry, is not desirable. The main driver of this over-approximation is the assumption that each task has static behaviour, meaning that independent of the computation the task's execution time is the same as the worst case execution time. However, in an implementation of a task the designer often can distuingish different internal states and their transitions leading to different worst case execution times. As an example assume a task that periodically polls the value of sensor with a high frequency, collects the data, smoothes the collected data after a fixed number of collected values, and finally sends out such precomputed value. Clearly, the amount of time used for collecting data is much smaller than the cumsumed time used for smoothing the data each n th invocation. Furthermore assume that this task has high priority in a fixed priority based preemptive scheduling. Each invocation of that task a conservative scheduling analysis must predict the worst case execution time regardless of its internal state, leading in a low accuracy of response times of tasks with lower priority. Another example is the internal structure of tasks in an AUTOSAR [7] driven development process, where a set of so-called runnables (pieces of executable code) are assigned to one task, but where external events define which runnable of a task is executed each time the task is invoked. Such requirements on the decision of which part of a task has to be executed are clearly functional.

In order to overcome these limitations of traditional scheduling analysis while preserving their scalability, we propose a new algorithm that unifies the advantages of statebased execution times and analytical methods. We will keep the principle of propagating activation pattern in a holistic analysis, like described in [8,5], but we will introduce a new type of analysis for a) response times of single tasks, and b) end-to-end delays of task chains. The analysis is capable of catering for functional constraints, given in terms of internal automaton for each task which defines the resource demand for computation in each state and allows us to achieve more accurate results. The tasks automata are allowed to send pre-defined events to other tasks connected to them in a task graph. Transitions in the task's automaton may be guarded by such events, which leads to the integration of functional behaviour even in the overall system. In the following we show how such flow of information can be exploited in the calculation of end-to-end delays of task chains.

This paper is structured as follows: We firstly will define a model of task graphs containing task automata. Afterwards the algorithm for analysing the response time of tasks under fixed priority preemptive scheduling is shown, followed its embedding in a holistic analysis in order to achieve results for end-to-end delays under functional constraints. Experimental results for a MPEG streaming case study will be used to evaluate our approach.

div.p: From the definition of a task it is clear, that we currently support only one outgoing communication, which is defined by the transitions of the state machine. Furthermore, we restrict all deadlines to be less or equal than the difference of two subsequent task activations. Beside the definition of the task internal state machine the parameters of a task are as they are in traditional approaches, like [10]. The semantics of the state machine is as follows:
• Whenever a task is invoked, a state change will occur immediately and this new state will hold until the task terminates. No state changes occur, when a task is preempted or blocked.
• Which transition to follow is decided on the available input communications and may be nondeterministic.
• If a task terminates,the output communication will be sent to the target tasks.

For simplicity reasons, we define that a task τ i may only be sensitive to an input set Σ i , if the producers of Σ i ⊆ COM send this communication directly to τ i , i.e. there exists a transition (s, I, s ′ , K, τ i ) ∈ T j of a task τ j , and Ω j ∩ Σ i = ∅. This allows us to simplify the encoding since we know on the one hand that the input communication sets of all tasks are disjoint. On the other hand, since we are in a setting, where no concurrent invocations of the same tasks are active, we know that at the point in time where τ i becomes invoked, its predecessor in the task chain has terminated. div.head: Response time analysis
div.p: With a given deployment Π the response time of each task in the task graph can now be calculated. In the following we will present this for a preemptive fixed priority scheduling, that returns an upper bound while considering the internal state machines of each task with higher priority than the task under analysis. The calculation is encoded in terms of a set of constraints, which is based on a) the discretisation of the time line according to the set ν, and b) an unrolling of the well known fix-point calculation usually used for response time analysis [10]. For deriving the response time of a task τ i in state s i ∈ S i we define the union of all event streams of tasks τ k with higher priority (prio(τ k )) than τ i , decorated by their internal states:

A similar set of constraints can be constructed for achieving a best case response time analysis. Due to page limitation we refrain on expanding on this here. In order to solve the above sketched constraint system, we produce an encoding of all constraints as a boolean satisfiability problem for the SAT checker HySAT [11], which leads to a set of (in-)equations over boolean variables. Because satisfiability checking cannot handle maximisation, we have to reduce the equation for r + τi (s j ) into a constraint, where the different values of k are represented by boolean variables B k , which are used to determine the upper bound of the unrolling of the response time calculation formalism:
div.formula: B k ↔ r + τ i (k -1, sj) > t k

div.formula: r + τ i (sj) = r + τ i (k, sj), s.t. B k ∧ ¬B k+1
div.p: Solving this system of (in-)equations by applying a SAT checker gives us either an unsatisfiability result, or a valuation for the given bound r on the response time. Obviously, this valuation may not be the worst case, but is just one valuation that satisfies the conjunction of all (in)equations. This result becomes sufficient, if it is used as feasibility check wrt. the task's local deadline by adding a further constraint r + τi (s j ) > d i . A result satisfiable indicates that there exists a worst case path which is longer than allowed by the deadline. In order to get a worst case response time 1 we embed the approach in a binary search, where a safe upper bound r is given and then we iteratively refine the bound until we reach a single point where no values greater than a satisfiable bound leads to a satisfiable valuation. In the end this gives us the worst case response time and, furthermore, the state of each preempting task invocation. In section 7 we will show some preliminary results of this approach.

div.head: Holistic analysis
div.p: Calculating the response time of a task by the approach described above (or even for other approaches) is based on assumptions about temporal activation properties of each task which may preempt the task under analysis. It is well known, that these assumptions are driven by the entire system and therefore a holistic analysis approach is needed, in which the activation properties of tasks triggered by messages coming from previously invoked tasks are propagated through the system, while influencing the response time of all tasks of the system. In the end we have to employ a fix-point on this propagation until we reach a state where no changes in the system occur anymore 2 . This is the usually used implementation of the analysis of distributed systems, where we directly can plug-in our response time analysis approach by replacing traditionally used analysis approaches. Thus we propose the following embedding: Activation properties of a task is characterised by a period and a release jitter. The period is inherited by the triggering task in a task chain, whereas the jitter is calculated by taking the maximal difference between best case and worst case response time, hence it holds:

div.head: Case study
div.p: In order to show the applicability of our approach let us define an example system, which is inspired from the case study given in [13]: Assume two sources of MPEG-2 streams using a bus system, and a third task chain polling a sensor. Figure 3 shows architecture and deployment. MPEG-2 stream 1 is served by the task chain τ 1 → τ 2 → τ 3 (from DVD to monitor), stream 2 is served by τ ′ 1 → τ ′ 2 → τ ′ 3 (from camera to hard disk), without any knowledge about their interleavings. The sensor is served by task chain τ 4 → τ 5 → τ 6 (from switch to display). The architecture consists of four processing nodes P 1 to P 4 and one bus P 5 .

As usually done in MPEG decoders, we a priori define a set of frame pattern that the stream is built from. Suppose that the following frame patterns are repeated in a stream: either IBBPBB, IBPBPB, or IBPB 3 . Each time a pattern has to be created, the content of the video information determines which pattern to choose. Each frame has to be sent in a time window of 250µs, before the next frame can be transmitted. Following this approach, the pattern behaviour can be encoded as a task automaton, see figure 4.

The states I, B and P represent the transmission of the very frames. Each branch the automaton determines nondeterministically which path to follow. The inputs of each 3 I frames have much data, P frames have less data, and B frames have minimal data. cf. [14] for more information about MPEG-2 encoding. transition are set to don't care, since we here want to decide on the type of frame 4 . The outputs are set to a value representing the chosen frame. This information is used to trigger the appropriate part of the decoder task. The entire task chain is shown in figure 5. Task τ 1 reads the input data from DVD and sends it to τ 2 , which serves the transmission of the frame pattern on P 5 . Afterwards τ 3 decodes the data and sends raw picture information to the monitor. Since each frame needs different amount of time to be decoded, we introduce states I, P and B in the automaton of task τ 3 . One common feature of MPEG-2 decoders is that they may decide to decode B frames or to skip them, because the calculation needed for decoding this kind of frames is very expensive. This is represented by the state N in τ 3 's automaton.

The second MPEG stream is served by simply copying task τ 1 to τ 3 with the same properties and automaton. The remaining part of our case study is a simple task chain that polls a sensor at P 2 , sends the information via P 5 to P 1 , and drives a display. The automata of this chain are outlined in figure 6.

The periods of the task chains used for serving the MPEG streams are set to 250µs. For the sensor task chain we define a period of 2ms. The worst and best case execution time for each task in each state is given in table 1.

div.p: 7 Experimental results

div.head: Applying the case study
div.p: In order to analyse the temporal behaviour of the case study presented in the last section, we first have to give a real-time requirement to be verified. The most interesting requirement is an end-to-end deadline for the task chain τ 4 → τ 5 → τ 6 , because in particular task τ 5 suffers preemption of both MPEG streams and therefore is appropriate to show the benefit of the automaton-based approach presented in the previous sections.

As requirement we define an end-to-end deadline of 2000µs for the mentioned task chain. Applying the holistic analysis as described in section 4 we yield response times for all task in all state within less than 3 minutes. Finally the requirement verification is applied by using the IPET encoding described in section 5 and returns a end-to-end response time of 520µs within less than 0.1 seconds, which is less than the specified deadline.

div.head: Comparison with other approaches
div.p: In order to assess the increase in accuracy of our approach in comparison to other approaches, two different purely analytical methods were applied to this example. The first analytical methods uses the traditional worst case assumption, meaning that each invocation of a task consumes its maximal worst case execution time, regardless of the internal behaviour. Hence for the MPEG streams transmitted on P 5 each invocation is assumed to be an I-frame, which in fact leads to a high over-approximation since due to the structure of the given frame pattern, I-frames are rarely sent. To do better for such specific structural properties like the small set of allowed pattern, Ernst et al. tried to give a more accurate analysis in [13], called intra-event streams. The idea behind this approach is the construction of an worst case sequence of patterns within a time interval, which is based on the possible set of pattern. For our example according to [13] the worst case sequence for each stream is IIIPPPBBBBBB 5 . The different degree of accuracy of all three approaches is shown in figure 7, where the response time of task τ 5 was compared. As can be seen, when considering the intra-event stream of [13] in the fourth invocation P-frames instead of I-frames are assumed to be transmitted. This leads to more slack time on P 5 which is filled by the execution of τ 5 and leads to a decreased response time (976µs instead of 1230µs). Our approach yields much better results, since a complete search on the possible interleavings defined by the internal automaton is computed; the worst case sequence that can be achieved is an I-frame followed by an B-frame, because no other sequence with higher cumulative load is possible. Again this leads to more slack time which can be used by τ 5 . In the end we predict a response time of 436µs, which is nearly 30% of the result of the traditional approach.

Since the example given in figure 7 is only a snapshot, a more systematical approach is needed in order to assess the benefit of our approach. An appropriate setting is achieved by increasing the worst case execution time of the task un-der analysis; this leads to more and more invocations of preempting tasks. For the sake of comparison all three methods were applied to the extended example. Figure 8 summerises the results in terms of the response time of task τ 5 , where the WCET of τ 5 was stepwise increased. automata approach approach from [13] traditional Beside the increasing benefit of both, the approach presented in [13] and the approach presented in this paper, for increasing WCET values, figure 8 indicates a further benefit of the automaton based approach, which converges to the response times yielded by [13]. This convergence can be explained by the fact that [13] produces an re-sorted list of the worst case occurrence of frames within the hyper-period (common least multiplier of the patterns period), which in fact our approach will find as worst case scenario for sufficient long response times. After this point of convergence the results again will differ as during the first hyper-period. Beside this single point of convergence the automaton based approach gives much better results, in average less than 2/3 of the response time predicted by [13]. However, [13] is mainly tailored to systems that define a small set of possible patterns, whereas our approach is able to treat arbitrary complex communicating automata. In particular in the case of causal dependent tasks preempting a task under analysis, the automata based approach is able to consider transitions to states which depend on the communication of predecessor tasks. Neither the traditional approach nor the approach presented in [13] are able to exploit this additional functional information.

div.head: Scalability
div.p: Obviously, the main drawback of searching for the worst case response time of a task without any abstraction is complexity: the encoding is fed into a boolean satisfiability checker, which theoretically needs exponential time for finding a solution. Though over the last decade there was fundamental progress towards efficient solvers, the observed complexity still depends on size and kind of problem to solve. In order to assess the efficiency of our approach in terms of run-times, we made numerous experiments, where it turns out that for complex automata with high numbers of invocations the longest run-times were observed; In fact the number of tasks -and even complex ones -is not as important for run-time as the number of their invocations. Figure 9 gives an overview on this observation, where we increase the considered number of invocation of preempting tasks while looking at the run-time of the slowest instance of the satisfiability check during binary search for response time calculation. The example again is based on the case study described in section 6. The exponential blow-up of the run-time for more invocations is caused by the two main drivers of complexity: the unrolling of complex automata and the unrolling of the fix-point equation for response time calculation. For higher numbers of invocations to be considered, both increase the number of boolean variables, which are one of the underlying reasons for complexity. For our example we observe them to be in the range of about 4000 for the setting that considers 4 invocations (run-time 0.14s) up to 37000 for the setting that considers 28 invocations (run-time 46.3s). Nevertheless, strict dependencies of many of the variables due to the specific encoding of our problem formalisation leads to reasonable run-times of the satisfiability checker. Moreover, our expectation is, that complex automata in conjunction with widely differing periods are quite seldom in embedded systems. In the end, it is the designers responsibility to find appropriate approximations in terms of internal automata for task's behaviour, where for systems fulfilling the above described criteria a trade-off between analysis complexity and accuracy has to be found. Beside this, several optimisations will be implemented in the future. For example, in [15] we addressed a different topic by a similar approach where some learning techniques during binary search are introduced. Such methods can be re-used here.

div.head: Application use cases
div.p: While the capability of calculating tighter response times was already shown in the previous section, in the following we will exemplify more advanced use cases considering functional dependencies.

div.head: Scenarios using system modes
div.p: System modes are used to separate different operational scenarios where different functions are active, which in our context boils down to define a system mode by a set of allowed states for each task. For example in an aircraft during landing a set of tasks are enabled, others are disabled; Or some tasks perform their actions in a degraded mode due to the loss of some sensors. In our environment this can easily be modelled by the following definition:

A System Mode SM ⊆ ∀τi∈T (S i ∪ s ∅ i ) is defined by a set of allowed states for each task. The set of states for each task is enriched by a special state in which the tasks don't consume any time; in this way we are able to model the absence of a task in some modes. Tasks which are not affected by a system mode can be represented by allowing all of their states. In this way we can combine different system modes SM 1 and SM 2 by simply building SM 1 ∩ SM 2 . Now its easy to define a specific analysis scenario, where we are, e.g., interested in the response time of a task τ i while system modes SM 1 and SM 2 are active, by excluding those state-based tuple in the cumulative event stream:
div.formula: ESS k -{(t, n, sj) ∈ ESS k | sj ∈ (Si -(SM1 ∩ SM2))}
div.p: In the same way this approach can be applied to the path analysis. It can also be used to forbid combinations of system modes in general. If the designer knows from his application that system modes SM 1 and SM 2 never can be active at the same time, than this can modelled by simply making these system modes visible in the encoding of the response time analysis by introducing boolean variables B SMi . Let B τi sj be a boolean variable indicating whether state s j of task i is active.
div.formula: ∀τi ∈ T : ∀sj ∈ (Si -SM1) : BSM 1 ⇔ X B τ i s j = 0 ∀τi ∈ T : ∀sj ∈ (Si -SM2) : BSM 2 ⇔ X B τ i s j = 0 BSM 1 + BSM 2 ≤ 1
div.p: Furthermore we can define this for more than one invocation of each task. Otherwise the analysis algorithm is allowed to change the modes in each invocation which is an unlikely scenario. Applying this to the analysis of the response time without the restriction of having different system modes active at the same time, we not only get the worst case response time of a task, but we also get the combination of system modes under which this response time occurs. This can be used to iteratively restructure deployment and design. Applying this to our example, we define two different operation modes SM 1 , SM 2 of our system. SM 1 is the normal operation mode, where all states of all tasks are allowed, except the N -states of task τ 3 and τ ′ 3 . SM 2 represents a degraded mode, where the decoding of the MPEG-2 streams are forced to skip the decoding of B-frames. Hence, SM 2 contains all states of all tasks, except the Bstates of task τ 3 and τ ′ 3 . If we now apply the response time analysis for both modes, we obtain, e.g., different response times for task τ 4 , which suffers preemptions of τ 3 : In SM 1 : r + τ4 = 72, whereas for SM 2 : r + τ4 = 58. This can easily be explained by the fact that state τ 3 .B in SM 2 is not allowed, hence the algorithm chooses the next most costly state which is P (14µs WCET instead of 28µs for state B).

div.head: Scenarios using functional constraints
div.p: The term functional constraints here means the observation of specific sequences of task outputs in a task graph. This kind of scenarios are not applied to response time analysis, but to the path analysis, because such sequences define the allowed interaction of tasks in a task graph. One graphical representation of such sequences of interactions can be sequence diagrams, as exemplified for our example in figure 10. The meaning here is that we are only interested in the end-to-end timing of the task graph under the assumption that the interactions occurring on the path are compliant to the interaction sequence specified in figure 10. This can be achieved by forcing those transitions in the IPET encoding of the task graph to be active which communicate the desired interaction. Hence for each task τ i which is constrained by a partial sequence τ i .O i we define: ∀sj ∈ T τ l ∈succ(τ i ) S l , ∀s k ∈ Si : Oi ∈ ω k i : P B ((τ k , s k ),(τ j , s j ),C) = 1

This encoding forces the search algorithm to choose one of those transitions that emit the desired interaction, whereas all other transitions are disabled due to the fact that in the IPET encoding the sum of all outgoing transitions of a task equals one. In this way we are able to restrict the set of possible paths through the task graph by functional constraints; it also allows us to specify different end-to-end timings for different scenarios. Applying this to our example, we introduce a sequence diagram showing the sequence of communication for a task chain under analysis. This sequence diagram is shown in figure 10. The vertical lines in figure 10 are instance lines representing active objects, i.e. tasks and the environment. The dashed lines represent flow of control, the solid lines flow of data and control. The meaning of this diagram is: whenever For the case study described in section 6 this leads to a response time of the task chain τ 1 → τ 2 → τ 3 of 158µs.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper we presented a new approach to the schedulability analysis under functional constraints, which is key in assessing the timing of complex distributed embedded systems, like for example coming out of an AUTOSARdriven process. The issue of taking task internal state machines into account during response time analysis was addressed by an encoding of both the computational state machine and the recurrent analytical response time calculation in a satisfiability problem, surrounded by a binary search method used for maximising the response time result. State based end-to-end delays can be calculated by an IPET-based encoding of the task graph with respect to the internal states and response times of each task in the graph. This setting gives us a powerful analysis environment, where we can apply different use cases, like interaction scenarios for the end-to-end analysis and system mode scenarios for the response time analyses. Furthermore, due to the event stream based encoding of discrete time instances in the response time analysis, this approach can easily be embedded in a holistic system analysis. Obviously this approach doesn't cover the complete range of system properties, thus for future work we plan to investigate more on how to incorporate cyclic task graphs and tree-shaped analysis. Furthermore we will investigate in how far we are able to incorporate hierarchical scheduling approaches, like periodic servers etc. From the requirements point of view we will assess to what extend we are able to generalise the requirements in terms of arbitrary sequence diagrams or finite state machines.
